sources.news_title: Tanker hits New Orleans cruise ship, 32 hospitalized
sources.text:
Police and tugboat crews rushed to help passengers escape a sinking riverboat on Friday after a tanker hit it at a New Orleans dock. The BBC reported that 32 people were hospitalized with injuries officials described as non-critical. Everyone aboard was accounted for.
The American Heritage was nearing the end of an eight-day cruise when the Atlantic Asphalt struck it. The port authority said the riverboat was carrying about 129 passengers as well as crew.
People began leaving the vessel as it leaned over, and it eventually came to rest on its side in the Mississippi River.
Authorities stopped river traffic during the rescue. New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno credited first responders and called the outcome a “miracle on the Mississippi."
Investigators are looking into what caused the crash. US Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said the tanker may have lost steering.

sources.news_title: Miracle on the Mississippi: Cruiser Topples and Sinks After Being Hit by Tanker, Everyone's OK
sources.text:
The incident unfolded at midday on Friday, November 13, when the American Heritage cruiser was docked at the Port of New Orleans. Documents cited by local media note that the riverboat had been tied up in the same position for two hours and was just letting passengers off, when the collision occurred.
Atlantic Asphalt, a tanker carrying asphalt owned by Chinese and Liberian companies but flagged in the Marshall Islands, crossed under the bridge and headed directly towards the cruiser, hitting it in the center of the hull. Even though the tanker had dropped anchor in the hope of slowing down, the impact was forceful enough to roll the riverboat over almost instantly.
The cruiser toppled and started to sink, as passengers were either thrown or jumped into the water. American Heritage has a 150-guest boarding capacity, but reports note that there were 200 people onboard, including crew members.
An investigation is now underway to determine the cause of the accident. First reports indicate that the tanker had an issue with steering, which prevented the captain from stopping or redirecting the vessel to prevent the collision. One of the guests on the cruiser told the media that crew on the tanker were "running around like ants" right before the moment of impact.
The American Heritage was a paddlewheeler built in 2015, part of the American Cruise Lines fleet. It was a five-deck vessel with a glass-enclosed restaurant, open-seat dining, and three guest lounges, as well as gorgeous accommodation and style "celebrating the Mighty Mississippi River."
Reports say the tanker smashed into the glass restaurant, with the bow piercing a gaping hole into it, through which water rushed in. It was a scene "like in the [movie] Titanic," one guest says, with the impact so powerful as to throw her across on the floor.

sources.news_title: What caused New Orleans tanker crash? What we know
sources.text:
Published November 14, 2026
Investigations are ongoing to find out why the tanker named Atlantic Asphalt "lost control" and collided with an anchored river cruise ship in New Orleans on Friday, resulting in the overturning of the cruise ship and passengers being dumped into the Mississippi River.
According to New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno, the tanker "lost control" before it crashed into the American Heritage operated by American Cruise Lines around 12:30 p.m. at the Port of New Orleans. According to U.S. Coast Guard Captain Melanie Burnham, the ship seemed to experience "some kind of loss of steering"; however, she emphasised that "the exact reason is not known yet." At that time, a river pilot was controlling the tanker.
The river cruise ship had been docked for about two hours before the crash and was unloading the passengers. The cruise ship started sinking and overturned, dumping the passengers into the cold waters.
Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry stated there was an “active investigation” going on since the government wanted to know “exactly what happened.” The NTSB is sending a team; however, the FAA nationwide ground stop could affect when the team can arrive. The Coast Guard is also working on the case.
The Crescent City Connection bridge has not been hit, although it was examined. The collision is being considered an accident rather than something that was done deliberately.
The Port of New Orleans has filed a lawsuit against the tanker’s owner, Nave Shipping SA, and manager Thome Ship Management for over $1 million due to the breach of safety regulations.

sources.news_title: 180 people rescued after tanker crashes into river cruise in Mississippi
sources.text:
Authorities have hailed a ‘miracle’ after all 180 passengers and crew on a tanker and river cruise boat were accounted for following a collision that left the pleasure vessel on its side.
An investigation has been opened after the Atlantic Asphalt tanker struck a parked American Heritage cruise in the Mississippi River at the port of New Orleans.
Experts say it is too soon to determine what caused the incident, but early evidence points to a catastrophic system failure onboard the tanker.
New Orleans mayor Helena Moreno told a news conference that 32 cruise passengers had been taken to hospital, none of whom were thought to have critical injuries.
‘We have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi,’ she said.
But she added many passengers had lost ID documents and mobile phones in the crash, meaning many were unable to contact their families.
She said a roll call conducted by American Cruise Lines in a nearby auditoriumaccounted for everyone not being treated in hospital.
Witnesses described seeing the tanker spinning out of control.
Port worker Devon Flanagan was left his truck as he saw passengers in the water, having escaped from the cruise, which had tipped onto its side.
‘It was just chaos,’ he recalled. ‘You had all types of ships, like other barges and other companies down there trying to help out, which also was a little convoluted because you had people still in the water.’
Coast guards closed a section of the Mississippi River to boat traffic as they conducted the rescue operation.
Martin Davies, a maritime law expert at Tulane University, said the tanker was sailing slowly upriver and against the current and had already safely cleared a difficult turn at Algiers Point.
‘For something like this to happen for an upbound ship indicates that something must have gone really badly wrong’, he said.
Mr Davies added that local pilots are used to provide guidance onboard vessels given their extensive knowledge of the waters.
The American Heritage cruise was at the end of an eight-day excursion of destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi.
According to the National Maritime Organisation, the tanker is owned by Nave Shipping SA, a company registered in Monrovia, Liberia.
This is a subsidiary of Chinese state firm China State Shipbuilding Corporation, which accounted for nearly a quarter of the gloabl shipbuilding market in 2022.
The Atlantic Asphalt vessel specialises in transporting large volumes of asphalt and bitumen, a semi-solid material used for roofing and in road construction.
An inquiry has been opened into the crash, but investigators from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) were delayed arriving at the scene after air travel was suspended across the US for five hours on Friday afternoon.

sources.news_title: River Cruise Ship With Nearly 200 People Aboard Capsizes After Tanker Strikes It In New Orleans
sources.text:
River Cruise Ship With Nearly 200 People Aboard Capsizes After Tanker Strikes It In New Orleans
Riverboat American Heritage capsized on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on November 13, 2026, after the tanker Atlantic Asphalt struck it while it was docked, sending 32 people to hospitals.
New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno told a news briefing that between 180 and 190 passengers and crew were on board, and all of them have been accounted for. She called the outcome a ‘miracle on the Mississippi’.
The collision took place at around 12:30 p.m. local time, according to the Port of New Orleans. The American Cruise Lines riverboat had docked about two hours earlier to let passengers disembark at the end of a weeklong cruise on the river.
The Marshall Islands-flagged tanker was northbound and had just passed under the Crescent City Connection bridge when it veered towards the riverfront. A local river pilot was reportedly on board the tanker at the time.
The commander of Coast Guard Sector New Orleans said the tanker appeared to have suffered some type of loss of steering. Investigators have not yet confirmed what caused the steering problem.
The tanker hit the American Heritage while passengers were still leaving the vessel. The riverboat began listing and rolled onto its side within minutes, which threw many people into the water.
The chief of the New Orleans Harbor Police informed that 87 people got off the vessel before it capsized. Her officers were the first to respond and entered the river to pull people to safety.
Firefighters extended ladders from the dock, and volunteer crews used their own boats to help in the rescue. The 32 people taken to hospitals included 30 passengers and two police officers, all with non-life-threatening injuries.
The American Heritage entered service in 2015 as the Queen of the Mississippi. It got its current name in 2022, when its operator added the word American to the names of its ships.
Vessel traffic on the river was stopped between mile markers 93 and 96 on Coast Guard orders while responders checked the site. The sector commander added that the riverboat is significantly damaged, with only a small part of it still above the waterline.
Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry promised to find out what went wrong and make the changes needed so that people can travel safely on the waterway.
The Coast Guard is investigating the collision along with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), which has sent a team to New Orleans.

sources.text:
A dramatic incident on the Mississippi River between a tanker and a cruise ship had many declaring it a “miracle” that there were no fatalities.
A docked river cruise boat with nearly 200 people on board was struck by a tanker Friday along the New Orleans waterfront, creating a surreal scene as the vessel tilted and began taking on water, sending passengers plunging into the river below.
WATCH: First responders rush to rescue passengers from a river cruise ship after a tanker slams into the docked vessel on the Mississippi River in New Orleans.
The American Heritage was carrying about 129 passengers when the collision occurred. Emergency crews are seen bringing people ashore as medical teams evaluate the injured, with local hospitals receiving an estimated two dozen patients.
New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno confirms all passengers have been accounted for, with no critical injuries reported.
The Coast Guard shut down a stretch of the river as rescue operations unfolded.
More on the collision and what officials are revealing about the response: https://t.co/mqGGfG6I0U
— Fox News (@FoxNews) November 13, 2026
The Atlantic Asphalt tanker hit the docked American Heritage cruise boat, which had just completed an eight-day cruise, after the tanker reportedly lost control.
“The boat started listing within minutes and flipped while emergency workers were still trying to get everyone off the ship,” according to the Associated Press, which reported 180 people aboard. “Dozens of people on board and at least two police officers were dragged from the 66-degree Fahrenheit (19-degree Celsius) river onto nearby ships.”
DRAMATIC FOOTAGE: Passengers clung to the side of a cruise ship as it rapidly rotated and began taking on water after colliding with an Atlantic Asphalt tanker on the Mississippi River near the Port of New Orleans. https://t.co/EsJfS6Weo7
— Breaking911 (@Breaking911) November 13, 2026
“Passengers were evacuating when the cruiser began taking on water and capsized, leaving some people in the river and others on a portion of the vessel still above water,” Fox News reported. “Harbor Police responded first, firefighters lowered ladders over the dock and nearby vessels helped pull people from the water.”
“We are throwing every asset we have to help rescue missing passengers,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a social media post. “Our prayers are with all those impacted by this terrible tragedy.”
NEW VIDEO: A passenger onboard the American Heritage River Cruise ship recorded this video of the oil tanker headed directly for them. This footage is unbelievable.
ABSOLUTELY TERRIFYING! https://t.co/T51lTUynSz
— Eric Spracklen (@EricSpracklen) November 13, 2026
And while certainly a harrowing incident, miraculously, all those aboard the cruise ship were accounted for.
“This is a miracle,” Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry said at a news conference. “The Mississippi River is not some quiet pond, right? I mean, there were challenges out there.”
“We have zero people unaccounted for, which is a miracle,” New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said, noting that 32 people had been taken to the hospital, none with critical injuries.
While the exact cause of the collision is unknown at this time, an investigation is underway, with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) dispatching a team.
Due to the residual delays from the nationwide ground stop, the NTSB will no longer send a board member and will instead send a team of investigators by ground to the scene of the vessel collision in New Orleans.
No media briefings are planned at this time. Updates on the investigation will be posted to this account and the investigation webpage:

— NTSB Newsroom (@NTSB_Newsroom) November 14, 2026
“We are getting everyone who was aboard the ship settled into hotels and making sure they have everything they need,” American Cruise Lines said. “We are also in close contact with the U.S. Coast Guard, New Orleans Police, and other agencies, and will continue to coordinate with them.”

sources.news_title: A tanker rammed the docked American Heritage near New Orleans, sending the riverboat into a complete capsizing—but all passengers and crew were accounted for
sources.text:
The Briefing:
- A Marshall Islands-flagged asphalt tanker, the Atlantic Asphalt, rammed the docked riverboat American Heritage on the Mississippi River near the Port of New Orleans on November 13, 2026.
- Thirty-two people were taken to local hospitals; no fatalities were reported and all aboard were accounted for.
- New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno and Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry each described the outcome as a "miracle on the Mississippi," given that the vessel capsized completely on a major river with more than 129 passengers and crew on board.
Tanker Loses Steering Before Impact
At approximately 12:30 p.m. CST on November 13, the 160-meter bitumen carrier Atlantic Asphalt veered into the stationary American Heritage at mile marker 96 along the lower Mississippi River. New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno told reporters at an evening press conference that the tanker had been moving out of control before it made contact with the paddlewheel vessel. USCG Captain Melanie Burnham, Deputy Commander of Sector New Orleans, said investigators had not yet pinpointed the exact reason behind the apparent loss of steering. The U.S. Coast Guard subsequently opened a formal inquiry, with mechanical failure listed among the possibilities but no conclusions drawn by Friday evening.
The American Heritage Had Just Arrived From Natchez
The American Heritage, an 81-meter paddlewheeler operated by American Cruise Lines with a capacity of 150 guests and a crew of roughly 40, had tied up at the port approximately two hours before the collision after a transit from Natchez, Mississippi. The vessel was at the dock so that passengers could disembark and explore the city. The Atlantic Asphalt, which had departed Paulsboro, New Jersey, on October 26, had been anchored at the Port of New Orleans since November 11—two days before the incident, according to vessel-tracking data reviewed by maritime outlet gCaptain.
Chaos on the Waterfront: Passengers Thrown Into the River
Video footage that spread rapidly across social media captured the full force of the impact as the tanker's hull met the cruise ship's broadside, sending the American Heritage into an immediate and violent list. Passengers who had already begun stepping off the vessel scrambled for safety on the dock, while others were thrown into the cold Mississippi. Emergency communications released by New Orleans Fire and Emergency Services captured the unfolding crisis in real time: "The boat just capsized — we have patients in the water."
New Orleans firefighters reached the scene within minutes, extending ladders over the dock to pull survivors to safety. Units from the Port Authority police, the city's fire department, and multiple U.S. Coast Guard detachments launched a coordinated mass-rescue operation that officials characterized as one of the most complex multi-agency responses the port had seen in years.
A Passenger Hero Jumps In to Save an 84-Year-Old
Amid the chaos, one vacationer aboard the American Heritage drew widespread praise after leaping into the river to pull an 84-year-old man to safety. Local officials highlighted the act of bravery at the evening press briefing, and footage of the rescue circulated widely across social media throughout the afternoon and into the night.
'A Literal Miracle on the Mississippi'
By Friday evening, the scope of both the disaster and the relief had come fully into focus. Mayor Moreno called the survival of everyone aboard "truly a miracle on the Mississippi," given that a vessel carrying upward of 180 people between passengers and crew had completely capsized on a major river. Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry echoed that assessment, describing the outcome as "a literal miracle on the Mississippi."
Thirty-two people were transported to area hospitals with minor to moderate injuries. No fatalities were confirmed, and all passengers and crew members had been accounted for by the time authorities held their evening briefing.
Investigation Open — Ship Remains Capsized
American Cruise Lines issued a statement confirming that the American Heritage was at the dock when the collision occurred, and said the company worked alongside local authorities throughout the evacuation effort. The vessel—originally built in 2015 by Chesapeake Shipbuilding and operated under the name Queen of the Mississippi before being rechristened American Heritage in 2022—has been a fixture of Mississippi River itineraries for more than a decade.
The Atlantic Asphalt remained at the site under Coast Guard supervision on Friday evening as salvage teams assessed how to address the capsized riverboat. No significant fuel or cargo spill had been reported as of that time, though environmental assessments were expected to follow in the coming days. "This incident continues to develop," New Orleans public safety officials stated, with coordination between multiple agencies ongoing.

sources.news_title: Tanker T-Bones Docked Cruise Ship On Mississippi River In New Orleans, Capsizing Vessel In Terrifying Crash
sources.text:
A massive asphalt tanker lost control and slammed into a docked luxury river cruise ship on the Mississippi River in New Orleans Friday afternoon, flipping the passenger vessel onto its side in a heart-stopping collision that sent people scrambling into the water, yet officials say everyone walked away in what they’re calling a “miracle on the Mississippi.”
The Marshall Islands-flagged Atlantic Asphalt, a roughly 500-foot bitumen tanker, was steaming upriver near the Crescent City Connection bridge around 12:30 p.m. when it veered hard to starboard and T-boned the American Heritage, a 295-foot paddlewheeler operated by American Cruise Lines that had docked about two hours earlier to let passengers disembark after an eight-day cruise.
Dramatic video circulating online shows the green-and-red tanker plowing into the white multi-deck riverboat amidships. Moments later, the cruise ship began listing, taking on water, and slowly rolling onto its side against the pier as onlookers filmed from the dock and emergency crews raced in.
About 129 passengers plus crew, roughly 180 to 200 people total in some estimates, were aboard the American Heritage. Roughly 87 got off before the vessel fully capsized. Others jumped into the river or clung to the high side as rescuers, including Harbor Police, firefighters, Coast Guard boats, and nearby vessels, pulled them to safety.
New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno confirmed at a Friday news conference that every passenger and crew member was accounted for with zero fatalities. Thirty-two people were taken to hospitals with non-critical injuries, including 30 passengers and two Harbor Police officers who went into the water during the rescue; some of those officers have since been released. No one on the tanker was hurt.
“We have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi,” Moreno said. Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry echoed the praise, calling the outcome a “literal miracle” given the river’s powerful currents and the scale of the crash.
Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said the tanker appeared to suffer “some type of a loss of steering,” though the exact cause remains under investigation. A river pilot was at the controls. Tracking data suggests the empty tanker was heading upriver to load cargo. The American Heritage is significantly damaged and partially submerged; salvage operations are underway.
The U.S. Coast Guard closed a stretch of the Mississippi between mile markers 93 and 96 to vessel traffic. Officials said they were working to reopen the waterway as soon as possible to keep commerce moving. The National Transportation Safety Board is sending investigators, delayed by residual effects of a nationwide FAA ground stop, and will lead the probe alongside the Coast Guard.
American Cruise Lines said guests and crew were evacuated and that the company is working with authorities. President Trump was briefed and praised the response.
For a few terrifying minutes under a clear blue sky, a routine disembarkation turned into a full-blown river disaster. Thanks to a rapid multi-agency response and a bit of luck, it ended with everyone alive.

All accounted for after tanker crashes into docked New Orleans riverboat
|                            Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...                        | 
A tanker ship struck a riverboat carrying nearly 200 people Friday in New Orleans, causing the cruise ship to capsize at its dock and prompting a wide-scale search and rescue operation, authorities said.
Mayor Helena Moreno of New Orleans said at a news conference that all passengers of the riverboat, the American Heritage, were accounted for after the crash. She added that 32 people were at local hospitals, none with critical injuries.
Capt. Melanie A. Burnham, commander of Sector New Orleans for the U.S. Coast Guard, praised the work of those who rescued the ship’s passengers.
“I want to recognize the dedication, professionalism and bravery of all those first responders,” she said.
“It is a literal miracle on the Mississippi,” said Gov. Jeff Landry of Louisiana, who also spoke at the news conference.
It was not clear what had caused the tanker, which officials identified as the Atlantic Asphalt, to lose control and veer into the side of the passenger boat, one of the paddle wheel vessels synonymous with the Mississippi River. Nor was it said what, if anything, the tanker was carrying.
The crash happened around 12:30 p.m. Central time Friday, sending passengers and crew members on the riverboat into the river.
People aboard clung to the rails and screamed as the riverboat overturned, according to videos posted online.
Others wrapped their arms around orange inflatable rings and bobbed in the water.
Wayne Hager III said his daughter, Leelah Hager, 19, had been working in housekeeping aboard the riverboat when it was struck.
She texted him about the crash, but he became worried when she stopped responding. She later made a video call to him.
When he answered, Leelah Hager appeared fully submerged in the river wearing a bright orange life jacket, he said.
His daughter was crying and told her father she was scared. He said he could see “hunks of metal” near her. The call dropped. Wayne Hager called back but only heard screams and yelling.
Leelah Hager called her father back later from land and said she was safe. She told her father that while in the water, she had helped a friend stay afloat who had not be able to don a life jacket correctly.
Jamie Holford, 42, was pulling up to the harbor parking lot around 12:30 p.m., he said, when he heard a tremendous noise.
“Imagine a giant Coke can, and you crushing it,” he said. “That’s about the easiest way I can explain that.”
Holford, who installs commercial kitchen equipment, had arrived with a fellow worker and was getting ready to board the ship itself to survey it for a new kitchen install in about a month.
He was about “40 yards, give or take,” from the scene of the crash but didn’t see the tanker itself hit the boat. He saw the “dock being rammed by the tanker,” he said.
A majority of the passengers seemed to have gotten off already, he said, by the time he got to the docks.
“It was starting to take on water,” he said. “It was tilting a little bit. We helped them get the catwalk back onto the dock whenever the boat drifted closer to the dock.
“Probably after about maybe 10 minutes, the boat just started rolling over,” he said.
The riverboat had been docked for two hours on the Mississippi River outside of 1350 Port of New Orleans Place, said Kimberly Curth, a spokesperson for the Port of New Orleans, and was just beginning to unload passengers. The river boat had arrived from Natchez, Mississippi, according to MarineTraffic, a ship tracking website.
The American Heritage can accommodate up to 150 passengers, according to American Cruise Lines. It has a glass-enclosed restaurant, guest lounges and a fitness center.

NEW ORLEANS – A tanker ship collided with an American Cruise Lines passenger ship that was docked in New Orleans on the Mississippi River on Nov. 13, and local TV showed passengers with life vests in the water.
The US Coast Guard said in an emailed statement that it had responded to the collision and that all river traffic was closed in the vicinity. It provided no other details.
Local TV also showed videos of the cruise ship listing on its side, while CBS News reported that at least 14 people had been rescued from the water.
The cruise ship has a capacity for 150 people and was built in 2015, American Cruise Lines said on its website.
The Advocate newspaper, citing unnamed Port of New Orleans officials, reported that 129 passengers were aboard the American Heritage cruise ship when it was hit by the Atlantic Asphalt, a tanker, at approximately 12:30 p.m. There was no immediate word on any deaths or injuries.
The Port of New Orleans did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
American Cruise Lines said in an emailed statement that it could confirm that its riverboat was involved in a collision.
"We are in close coordination with the US Coast Guard and local authorities. Guests and crew were evacuated, and we are deeply concerned for everyone involved. We will share more information as it becomes available," the company said.
US Army officer accused of spying for Russia identified
The U.S. Army officer arrested in the United Kingdom on suspicion of attempting to spy for Russia was a human rights specialist assigned to NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps, two U.S. officials said.
The suspect, Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, 41, was arrested in a sting operation on Nov. 10, and British authorities are expected to charge him in the coming days, according to one of the officials.
After he is charged in the UK, the U.S. military intends to prosecute Tyner in the United States under the Uniform Code of Military Justice, the official said, adding that the Pentagon would collaborate with the Justice Department.
London Metropolitan Police said the arrest followed an investigation by its counter terrorism unit in collaboration with the FBI and the U.S. military.
Tyner, who has served in the Army since 2008, was deployed to Afghanistan, Iraq and Qatar. It was not immediately clear what Tyner's motive was, but one official said he is not believed to have shared any intelligence with Russian authorities.
Microsoft services mostly fixed after 24-hour outage
A worldwide Microsoft outage has stabilized after more than 24 hours, during which thousands of users couldn't access their emails, apps and other services.
"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," Microsoft stated in a post on X Friday afternoon, Nov. 13. "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously."
Microsoft also confirmed that the outage was not due to a cyberattack and added that it has "addressed the underlying issue and continues to restore service to remaining customers and regions."
Downdetector received 1,600 reports of issues with Outlook, Microsoft's email service, as of 2:50 p.m. ET, down from the 130,000 reported when the outage started Thursday, Nov. 12. Microsoft 365, meanwhile, reported to 700 around the same time, down from a peak of nearly 50,000.
US denies Iran's claim that it attacked early-warning radar in Bahrain
The US military denied Iran's claim Nov. 13 to have attacked a US early-warning radar in Bahrain, saying its forces had shot down two one-way attack drones launched by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps toward Bahrain with no harm caused.
Iran had said its strike was in retaliation for what it described as an air attack on a telecommunications tower in its Hormozgan province, according to Iranian state media.
The claim came during a fragile lull in the conflict between Iran and the US, which began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28 and has since spread across the region.
Iran launched missile and drone attacks on US bases in Gulf states and sought to restrict shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for global oil and gas supplies. Washington, in turn, imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports.
There was no immediate comment from Bahrain.
A man thought he was eating a sweet treat. It turned out to be a bomb
A 35-year-old man in India died after a homemade explosive device, a bomb disguised as a traditional dessert, detonated inside his mouth, according to reports citing authorities.
Police in Madhya Pradesh identified the victim as 35-year-old Rajendra Barautiya, according to India Today.
Another outlet, The Indian Express, said that Rajendra Barautiya was sitting at a bonfire with his family after dinner Tuesday evening, Nov. 10, in the courtyard of his home in Padariya Chhanta village. A neighbor arrived and joined him near the fire, Dindori Kotwali Inspector Durga Prasad Nagpure told the newspaper.
The outlet also reports that during their conversation, the neighbor allegedly offered Rajendra what he described as a rasgulla, a popular Indian dessert consisting of soft, round cheese dumplings soaked in sugar syrup.
Police said the device was a homemade explosive used in some rural communities to kill wild boars, according to The Indian Express. The devices are reportedly made by packing gunpowder into balls of dough. The device detonated when Rajendra bit into it, leaving him with severe injuries to his mouth and jaw, police said.

Watch: Tanker hits docked river cruise boat in New Orleans
All passengers survive as Louisiana governor hails 'miracle on the Mississippi'
A tanker ship collided with a river cruise boat docked in New Orleans on Friday, causing it to capsize, but all of the roughly 180 people aboard were accounted for, officials said.
The American Heritage, a riverboat operated by American Cruise Lines that had been docked for about two hours in the Mississippi River, was hit by the Atlantic Asphalt tanker.
Despite the fact that passengers were disembarking at the time of the collision, which took place at about 12:30 pm (1830 GMT), there were no fatalities.
"This is a miracle. It is a literal miracle on the Mississippi," Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry told reporters.
Thirty-two people were taken to local hospitals for treatment, but none had suffered critical injuries, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno told a press conference.
Two of those hospitalised were police officers who were helping with the evacuations, she added.
Moreno put the total number of people on the river cruiser at between 180 and 190.
American Cruise Lines confirmed the incident in a statement, adding: "Guests and crew were evacuated, and we are deeply concerned for everyone involved."
In a later statement, it said: "We are getting everyone who was aboard the ship settled into hotels and making sure they have everything they need."
It was not immediately clear why the tanker collided with the river cruiser, which had docked about two hours before the collision.
First responders evacuated approximately 87 people from the cruise ship before it turned on its side, Moreno said.
"We have zero people unaccounted for," she added.
US President Donald Trump thanked Landry for his "outstanding leadership during this very agonising period of time," in a post on his Truth Social platform.
The Mississippi River was closed to vessel traffic in the area of the incident.
The US Coast Guard and the National Transportation Safety Board launched an investigation into the crash.

Trump praises Coast Guard, first responders for rescue efforts after tanker-cruise ship collision in Louisiana
New Orleans [US], November 14 (ANI): US President Donald Trump on Friday (local time) praised the United States Coast Guard, law enforcement agencies and emergency responders for their rescue efforts after a tanker collided with an American Cruise Lines riverboat on the Mississippi River in New Orleans, leaving 32 passengers hospitalised.
No casualties were reported in the incident.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump said, “Thank you to the United States Coast Guard for doing such an incredible job of rescue and other work, having to do with the crash of the two ships in Louisiana. Likewise, all of Law Enforcement and First Responders were fantastic! Incredibly, nobody was killed by this major collision. 32 people are in the hospital. Thank you to Governor Jeff Landry for your outstanding leadership during this very agonising period of time.”
The Atlantic Asphalt tanker collided with American Cruise Lines' American Heritage at around 12:30 pm on Friday while the riverboat was docked near the Port of New Orleans. The impact caused the passenger vessel to begin sinking before it eventually toppled over and flipped, according to New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno.
“The passengers began disembarking from the (American Cruise Lines) ship after that collision, but while that was happening, the cruise ship began to sink, and then eventually the cruise ship toppled over and flipped,” Moreno said during a news conference. “Now, when that occurred, we started to have people in the water.”
Moreno confirmed that 32 passengers were taken to local hospitals, with none suffering critical injuries. “At this moment, the information that we have, we have zero people unaccounted for,” she said, describing the outcome as a “miracle.”
US Coast Guard Captain Melanie Burnham said the tanker appeared to have experienced “some type of a loss of steering,” although authorities were yet to establish the “exact reason why.” She added that the person operating the tanker was a river pilot.
The Coast Guard said all passengers had been accounted for, with no reported casualties. It initially closed the Mississippi River to vessel traffic between mile markers 93 and 96 to facilitate rescue operations and ensure the safety of responders.
“We’re going to get the river opened as soon as possible so we can keep commerce flowing,” Burnham said, adding that authorities would likely allow one-way traffic initially.
The Coast Guard is coordinating with salvage teams to remove the damaged vessel and reopen the waterway, while investigations into the collision continue.
American Cruise Lines confirmed that guests and crew aboard the American Heritage had been evacuated and said it was coordinating with the Coast Guard and local authorities.
Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry said he was in close contact with local officials and law enforcement following the incident. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin also said federal agencies were coordinating with the state and deploying resources to support rescue efforts. (ANI)

sources.news_title: Tanker collides with cruise ship on Mississippi River, injuring 32 in New Orleans
‘Miracle’: All rescued from capsized New Orleans riverboat in tanker collision
sources.text:
Over 30 people were injured after a tanker collided with a docked riverboat on the Mississippi River near the Port of New Orleans, officials said Friday.
Nearly 200 people were on board the cruise ship, American Heritage, when the Atlantic Asphalt tanker collided with it, according New Orleans officials. All have been accounted for, according to New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno, calling it a “miracle on the Mississippi.”
Thirty passengers from the cruise ship and two officers who ended up the water are hospitalized with non-critical injuries, according to officials. No children were involved, authorities said.
The emergency response began midday Friday, when the tanker “lost control and collided into the cruise ship,” Moreno said.
“The passengers began disembarking from the ship after that collision. But while that was happening, the cruise ship began to sink, and then eventually, the cruise ship toppled over and flipped,” she said at a news conference Friday afternoon. “Now, when that occurred, we started to have people in the water.”
Police began helping evacuate passengers, though not everyone was able to get off before the ship began to capsize, authorities said. The remaining passengers were taken onto various boats to get them to safety, and the search and rescue effort is now over, authorities said.
Moreno praised the rescue effort involving first responders and volunteers.
“At this moment, the information that we have, we have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi, and that is a credit to all of the first responders, local, state, federal, who literally jumped right in to help,” she said.
The collision occurred at approximately 12:30 p.m. local time Friday, according to the Port of New Orleans. The tanker struck the riverboat broadside and hard, sources said.
The tanker appears to have had “some type of a loss of steering,” Burnham said during Friday’s news conference.
“The exact reason why, we don’t know that,” she said.
The cruise ship is “significantly damaged,” with a small portion remaining above the water line, according to U.S. Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham.
The incident remains under investigation, Burnham said. The National Transportation Safety Board also said it is launching a team to investigate and should arrive by Saturday morning.
“We are going to get down to the bottom of exactly what happened here, and make sure that we make any adjustments necessary so that the people that travel on the waterways here can can know that they can do so in safety,” Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry said at the news conference.
The riverboat had docked approximately two hours earlier to begin passenger disembarkation, according to the Port of New Orleans.
An American Heritage crew member told ABC News that he felt the boat shake, and initially thought the captain was moving the boat.
“There was a hole with the hull of the other boat in the dining room,” said Zayvion, a restaurant manager who did want his last name published. “It was a little chaotic, but our team knew what we were doing.”
Zayvion said the crew trains weekly for such a scenario and the team “just stayed calm” and helped guide shaken-up guests to safety.
“A lot of people were just scared, like what’s gonna happen, especially as the boat tipped over,” he said. “It was scary for a lot of people. Even me, like, when it was tipping, I was like, it was getting real.”
American Cruise Lines, the riverboat’s operator, said in a statement following the operation that it is “grateful to the U.S. Coast Guard, our crew, and the local first responders on the ground in New Orleans for their tremendous rescue efforts.”
“We are getting everyone who was aboard the ship settled into hotels and making sure they have everything they need,” the statement continued. “We are also in close contact with the U.S. Coast Guard, New Orleans Police, and other agencies, and will continue to coordinate with them.”
Multiple agencies, including the New Orleans Fire Department, the New Orleans Police Department and the U.S. Coast Guard, responded to the scene, officials said.
“The river is closed to all vessel traffic between mile markers 93 and 96 while responders assess the situation and conduct response operations,” the U.S. Coast Guard said.
Burnham said the Coast Guard will be evaluating how to reopen the waterway.

A nationwide FAA ground stop has delayed investigators travelling to New Orleans to probe a collision between a Chinese-owned tanker and a river cruise boat that left the passenger vessel capsized in the Mississippi River.
The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) was initially unable to send investigators to the scene after communications problems at regional air traffic control centres grounded flights nationwide on Friday, 13 November, according to the Associated Press.
The collision involved the tanker Atlantic Asphalt and the American Heritage, a river cruise boat carrying 180 passengers and crew members in total. All aboard survived the incident, although 32 people were taken to hospital with non-critical injuries, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno confirmed.

The Atlantic Asphalt struck the American Heritage while the cruise boat was docked in New Orleans, prompting a major rescue operation.
Footage from the scene showed the much larger tanker hitting the passenger vessel, with the impact causing significant damage. The American Heritage began listing within minutes before eventually overturning as emergency crews worked to evacuate those aboard.
Tugboat operators, port workers, police officers and other nearby rescuers rushed to help passengers and crew members who had fallen into the Mississippi River.
Moreno confirmed that nobody was unaccounted for following the incident, describing the outcome as 'a miracle on the Mississippi.'
Those who were not injured were taken to a nearby auditorium, where American Cruise Lines officials conducted a roll call to ensure everyone had been accounted for.
Many people reportedly lost personal belongings, including identification documents and car keys. City officials also arranged assistance with accommodation, food and transportation for those affected.

sources.text:
A tanker ship lost control and slammed into a docked American Cruise Lines paddlewheeler in the Port of New Orleans Friday afternoon, capsizing the vessel and dumping passengers into the Mississippi River in a rescue operation that ended with an outcome officials are calling the "miracle on the Mississippi."
The Atlantic Asphalt, a tanker flagged in the Marshall Islands, struck the American Heritage around 12:30 p.m. local time while the riverboat was tied up near the French Quarter, according to CBS News. The Heritage had docked roughly two hours earlier for passengers to disembark. New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said the tanker "lost control" before the collision.
As passengers were stepping off, the riverboat began to sink, then rolled and flipped, sending people into the water, the mayor said. CBS News reported that nearby boats pulled more than a dozen people from the river, and private vessels that happened to be on the water at the time joined the response as volunteers.
In a late-afternoon briefing, Moreno delivered the word that matters: "We have 0 people unaccounted for." Thirty-two passengers were taken to area hospitals, she said, none with critical injuries. New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said two of her officers were hospitalized during the rescue and were in good condition. No one aboard the tanker was hurt, according to CBS News. The New York Times reported one person suffered serious injuries, and NBC News put the total number of people aboard the Heritage at between 180 and 190, including crew. The passenger count circulated by Port NOLA and cited in the mayor's briefing was about 129.
"After the initial crash, it hit us again and we flipped over and I had to crawl over the railing and people to save myself," passenger Rhonda Akers told NBC News.
Witness Jamie Holford told CBS News he saw the Heritage hit the dock after the collision and watched people hurry off the boat before it rolled, with some climbing over the railing as the vessel went down.
Gov. Jeff Landry, speaking at the same briefing, called it "a literal miracle on the Mississippi," per the Times. Coast Guard Capt. Melanie A. Burnham, commander of Sector New Orleans, praised the "dedication, professionalism and bravery of all those first responders," the Times reported.
The response drew Port NOLA Harbor Police, the New Orleans Fire Department, the New Orleans Police Department and the U.S. Coast Guard. A three-mile stretch of the river was closed to traffic while responders worked, and a Coast Guard official said authorities were pushing to reopen the waterway as soon as possible.
The cause of the crash is under investigation. Moreno said it was not yet clear why the tanker lost control. The Coast Guard and the National Transportation Safety Board will conduct the probe — and NBC News reported that transportation officials were delayed reaching the city because of a ground stop at airports across the country.
Video circulating online Friday captured the moment of impact and its aftermath. Instagram accounts posted reels showing the tanker striking the docked cruise ship and the vessel listing in the river; the posts carried captions describing the collision, and the footage showed people in life jackets near the rails as the boat went over. Next News Network's own post on X noted the mayor's briefing figure directly: "we have 0 people unaccounted for" after a tanker slammed into a docked river cruise ship carrying about 129 passengers, with 32 sent to hospitals and none critical.
Port NOLA is one of the nation's largest ports, and the Mississippi at New Orleans is a working commercial channel where deep-draft tankers, barges and passenger boats share water every day. Friday's collision put a cruise vessel and an asphalt tanker in the same patch of river at the same moment, and the margin between a rescue story and a body count came down to docked ship's crew, professional first responders and civilians who steered toward people in the water.
Our Take
Here's what Friday actually proved. When the alarm went out, nobody asked what party the mayor belonged to, which agency had jurisdiction, or which newsroom would get the credit. Harbor cops went in the water. Fire crews went in the water. Private boaters who were just passing through on a Friday afternoon turned their hulls toward strangers in life jackets and pulled them out. Two Harbor Police officers ended up in the hospital doing it. That is what a country looks like when it still works.
So spare us the usual aftermath. Within hours of a Marshall Islands-flagged tanker putting 129 passengers in the Mississippi, the same crowd that lectures Americans about infrastructure and regulation will be warming up the hearings and the finger-pointing. Fine — the Coast Guard and NTSB should get answers on how a tanker "loses control" in one of the busiest port channels in the country. But the story America should be repeating this weekend isn't about a federal agency. It's about the fact that a paddlewheeler full of tourists flipped over in the Mississippi and every single soul came home.
"Miracle on the Mississippi" is the right phrase. Now the question for the investigators is simple: was Friday a miracle, or was it luck — and what has to change at the Port of New Orleans so the next tanker that loses control doesn't get a second chance at a boat full of families?

sources.news_title: Tanker Hits Docked Riverboat in New Orleans, 32 Hurt
sources.text:
A tanker that Coast Guard officials said appeared to lose steering struck a docked river cruise ship on the Mississippi River at the Port of New Orleans on Friday, and the ship capsized as passengers were disembarking, but officials said everyone aboard both vessels was accounted for and no deaths were reported. Thirty-two passengers were taken to hospitals with injuries that officials described as not critical, and eight remained hospitalized in the latest update. Two harbor police officers who took part in the rescue were also hospitalized and were in good condition. New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said the tanker "lost control" before it hit the American Heritage, and Gov. Jeff Landry called the outcome "a literal miracle on the Mississippi." The cause of the collision has not been determined and is under investigation by the Coast Guard and the National Transportation Safety Board.
The Atlantic Asphalt hit the American Heritage, a riverboat operated by American Cruise Lines, at about 12:30 p.m. local time, according to the Port of New Orleans. The collision happened near mile marker 96 of the Mississippi River, outside 1350 Port of New Orleans Place, near the French Quarter. The riverboat had docked about two hours earlier and had begun to disembark passengers. Officials first reported about 129 passengers aboard, along with crew members, and Moreno later estimated that 180 to 190 people were on board.
Moreno said that after the tanker struck the boat, passengers began leaving, but the vessel "began to sink, and then eventually toppled over and flipped." Videos from the scene showed the much larger tanker towering over the paddlewheel boat as metal and glass crumpled, and then the five-story vessel lying on its side and largely submerged. Some people were seen in the water wearing life jackets, and others stood near the railing as the high side of the ship tilted farther into the river. Early reports said at least 12 people were in the water, and nearby boats reported pulling more than a dozen people from the river.
Passengers were taken to the Port of New Orleans administration building for medical evaluation and assistance. Moreno said 32 passengers were hospitalized, and the LCMC Health system said it was treating them. She described the rescue as an "all hands on deck" effort that involved the New Orleans Fire Department, the New Orleans Police Department, the Coast Guard, harbor police, nearby boat operators and volunteers. Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said two of her officers were hospitalized during the operation. Moreno said no children were aboard and no injuries were reported on the tanker. American Cruise Lines confirmed the collision in a statement and said its immediate priority was the safety of passengers, crew members and first responders, and the company said it was coordinating with the Coast Guard and local authorities.
Many passengers lost phones, identification and other belongings, and officials worked to arrange replacement prescriptions, transportation and ways to contact relatives. Lt. Gov. Billy Nungesser secured 85 hotel rooms, and 50 to 60 passengers remained in hotels, according to WDSU. American Cruise Lines said it was housing passengers in hotels.
The Coast Guard closed the Mississippi River to vessel traffic between mile markers 93 and 96 while crews responded, and the Port of New Orleans advised vessels to avoid the affected section. The tanker has since been towed away, but part of the river was still closed Friday night, according to WDSU, and the Regional Transit Authority has resumed ferry service. Moreno said it could take weeks to remove the American Heritage from the river. Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said she was working to reopen the river. The Port of New Orleans is one of the nation's largest ports, and the closure affects traffic on one of the country's main commercial waterways.
Burnham told reporters the tanker appeared to have suffered some type of loss of steering, but she said officials do not yet know the exact reason why. The person at the helm was a river pilot, she said, and she had no indication the collision was terrorism-related. The Coast Guard and the NTSB are investigating. The NTSB said it would send a "Go Team," but because of residual delays from Friday's nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop, its investigators would travel by road and a board member would not go to the scene. Moreno said some investigators were already in New Orleans and others were expected Saturday. Officials have not said what caused the apparent loss of steering.
The Atlantic Asphalt is a 160-meter (520-foot) tanker, built in 2017 and registered in the Marshall Islands, according to MarineTraffic and its ship manager, OSM Thome. It specializes in carrying large quantities of asphalt and bitumen, a semi-solid material used in road construction and roofing. The tanker was bound for New Orleans, and officials have not said whether it was carrying cargo. The statements reviewed did not describe any spill from the tanker or damage to its cargo.
The American Heritage was built in 2015, has five decks and can carry up to 150 passengers. American Cruise Lines operates paddlewheel riverboats on the Mississippi and other rivers, and another Mississippi River cruise operator, Riverboat Twilight, posted a message saying its thoughts were with those affected.
The collision adds to a series of ship accidents on the lower Mississippi. In April 2025, the tanker Isla de Bioko collided with the towboat Ginny Stone near New Orleans, and the river was closed to traffic and later reopened. Friday's crash comes nearly 30 years after the freighter Bright Field hit the New Orleans riverfront in 1996.
The tanker struck the American Heritage at about 12:30 p.m. Friday, about two hours after the riverboat docked, with an estimated 180 to 190 people aboard. Everyone aboard both vessels was accounted for and no one was killed. Thirty-two passengers were taken to hospitals, eight of them still hospitalized in the latest update, and the American Heritage could take weeks to remove from the river.

sources.news_title: All passengers accounted for after tanker strikes river boat near New Orleans
sources.text:
(OSV News) — The Archdiocese of New Orleans called for prayer as emergency responders raced to save dozens of passengers on a river boat that was struck by a tanker on the Mississippi River near New Orleans around 12:30 p.m. Nov. 13.
Some 200 passengers and crew were believed to be on the American Heritage — a paddlewheeler craft operated by American Cruise Lines — when the river boat, which had docked some two hours earlier, was struck by the Atlantic Asphalt tanker.
According to officials, all passengers were later accounted for, with 30 passengers and two officers hospitalized for injuries deemed noncritical.
Speaking at a Nov. 13 news conference, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno called the lack of serious and fatal casualties a “miracle on the Mississippi.”
Collision saw ship quickly take on water and list
The broadside, high-impact collision saw the ship quickly take on water and list, causing the vessel to quickly capsize.
In a Facebook post uploaded minutes after the crash, the Archdiocese of New Orleans invoked the intercession of Mary as patroness of those who traverse the waters.
“Stella Maris, pray for us!” said the archdiocese. “Through the intercession of Our Lady, Star of the Sea, may all those aboard the river boat and all those working to rescue them be kept safe!”
Shortly thereafter, Archbishop James F. Checchio of New Orleans posted a statement on Facebook, saying, “Please join me in praying for everyone involved in today’s collision on the Mississippi River, their families, and the first responders working at the scene.
‘May the Lord protect all those affected’
“I have been in touch with the Governor’s office and city leaders to offer any assistance we can,” said Archbishop Checchio. “May the Lord protect all those affected, bring them comfort and peace, and keep everyone safe from further harm.”
Speaking to ABC News Nov. 13 in the early moments of the rescue, Louisiana’s Lt. Gov. Billy Nungesser admitted, “I’m fearing it could be pretty bad,” noting that river cruises are popular with senior citizens.
A number of media outlets had posted images of several passengers seen in the water wearing life jackets.
Gina Christian is a multimedia reporter for OSV News. Follow her on X @GinaJesseReina.

sources.text:
New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said Friday that every passenger and crew member aboard a river cruise ship was accounted for after an asphalt tanker lost control and capsized the vessel on the Mississippi River.
Thirty-two passengers were taken to area hospitals, none with critical injuries, Moreno said. No one was killed. About 129 passengers, along with crew members, were aboard the American Heritage when the tanker hit it.
Moreno addressed the outcome at an evening news conference.
“We have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi,” she said.
The Atlantic Asphalt hit the American Heritage at about 12:30 p.m. while the riverboat sat at the dock, the Port of New Orleans said. It had tied up about two hours earlier to let passengers off. Then the tanker hit. The riverboat took on water and rolled onto its side. New Orleans Fire and Emergency Services later released the radio traffic from around the time of the collision. On it, a responder reports a riverboat taking on water steadily.
Passengers went into the river as the ship turned over. Some surfaced in life jackets. Others climbed the railings as the deck tipped toward the water. Boats already on the river pulled more than a dozen people out, and the mayor said private vessels in the area responded as volunteers.
Jamie Holford watched the riverboat strike the dock and told CBS News that people hurried off before it rolled.
“It looked like something off the Titanic,” he said.
Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry flew to New Orleans. He told reporters the outcome was a literal miracle and pointed to the ages of the passengers aboard. Landry said he got Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on the phone first. Mullin was sworn in as DHS secretary in March.
President Donald Trump called soon after, the governor said, and offered the state whatever it needs.
The tanker runs 160 meters, roughly twice the length of the 81-meter paddlewheeler it hit. Tracking data shows it reached New Orleans on Nov. 11 out of Paulsboro, New Jersey.
The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) dispatched a Go Team to the scene for Saturday morning. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) grounded every flight in the country Friday afternoon over a communication problem at air traffic control centers, and Rep. Troy Carter (D-LA) said the halt was holding the investigators up.
“I know they are desperately trying to get here,” Carter told WDSU.
Landry said an active investigation is underway. The Coast Guard closed the river to all vessel traffic between mile markers 93 and 96.

sources.news_title: All passengers and crew on New Orleans paddleboat survive crash with tanker on Mississippi River
sources.text:
NEW ORLEANS (AP) — A tanker in New Orleans that apparently lost its steering slammed into a docked river cruise boat with 180 people aboard Friday, the mayor said. All aboard survived after the crash prompted a massive rescue operation for passengers and crew who plunged into the Mississippi River as the ship took on water and began to topple over.
Video from the scene showed the much larger Atlantic Asphalt tanker hit the American Heritage cruise boat while it was docked as metal and glass crashed and crunched.
Tugboat operators, nearby workers, police and other rescuers rushed to help.
“We have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi,” New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said at a news conference as rescuers and others cheered.
The mayor said 32 people were taken to the hospital, but none of them had critical injuries.
Ship started listing within minutes
The boat started listing within minutes and flipped while emergency workers were still trying to get everyone off the ship.
Dozens of people on board and at least two police officers were dragged from the 66-degree Fahrenheit (19-degree Celsius) river onto nearby ships.
Devon Flanagan was at his job nearby at the Port of New Orleans when workers rushed down the dock. He got out of his truck and saw the ship on its side and passengers in the water.
“It was just chaos,” he said. “You had all types of ships, like other barges and other companies down there trying to help out, which also was a little convoluted because you had people still in the water.”
It appeared the tanker seemed to have “some type of loss of steering,” but the exact cause of the crash was unknown, Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said.
The National Transportation Safety Board planned to investigate the crash, but members were initially unable to make it to New Orleans because all flights nationwide were grounded due to communications problems at regional air traffic control centers.
Cruise line did a roll call to make sure all were accounted for
The people who weren't injured were brought to a nearby auditorium, and cruise officials did a roll call to make sure everyone was accounted for, Moreno said.
Many people lost their IDs and even car keys in the disaster. Most were from out of town, the mayor said.
“They needed chargers for their phones. Some people didn’t have phones,” Moreno said. “This has now made national news. They need to contact their families to let them know they’re OK. Food, hotel rooms, transportation.”
The cruise ship was built in 2015 and operated by American Cruise Lines. It is five stories and can hold up to 150 passengers.
The American Heritage was finishing an eight-day cruise to several Mississippi River destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi.
The 520-foot-long (160-meter-long) vessel had a final destination in New Orleans, according to MarineTraffic, and was sailing under a flag for the Marshall Islands.
Expert says catastrophic failure of systems on boat
It's too early to tell what might have caused the crash, but videos indicate some kind of catastrophic system failure on the vessel and “super bad luck” that it struck the boat as passengers were departing, said Martin Davies, a maritime law expert at Tulane University.
The tanker was traveling upriver, going slowly against the current, Davies said.
“For something like this to happen for an upbound ship indicates that something must have gone really badly wrong,” Davies said.
Tankers have local pilots on board for guidance because they know the waters and the ship very well, and the ship had already made the difficult Algiers Point turn on the Mississippi River before it crashed, Davies said.
Tanker owned by subsidiary of Chinese shipbuilder
The ship is owned by a company called Nave Shipping SA, which is registered in Monrovia, Liberia, according to the International Maritime Organization.
It is a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation, a sprawling Chinese state-owned conglomerate, according to the live shipping tracker MarineTraffic.
The Chinese company overseeing the asphalt tanker in 2022 accounted for nearly a quarter of the global commercial shipbuilding market, according to a report by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. It was also the largest military shipbuilder in the world at the time.
China State Shipbuilding Corp. didn’t respond to an emailed request for comment Friday afternoon.
The tanker involved in the crash specializes in carrying large quantities of asphalt and bitumen, a semi-solid substance that is often used for road construction and roofing, according to MarineTraffic.
Jeffrey Collins reported from Columbia, South Carolina. Ed White in Detroit, Safiyah Riddle in Los Angeles, M Reo in Washington, D.C., Anna Wilder in Austin, Texas, and Beatrice Dupuy in New York contributed to this report.

A massive asphalt tanker collided with a docked paddlewheel cruise ship carrying roughly 129 passengers on the Mississippi River in New Orleans Friday afternoon, tipping the riverboat onto its side and triggering a frantic multi-agency water rescue.
More than a dozen people have reportedly been hospitalized as emergency crews work urgently to account for everyone who was aboard.
How the Crash Unfolded
The collision happened around 12:30 p.m. local time near the Crescent City Connection bridge, right outside the Port of New Orleans Administration Building.
- The Impact: The 520-foot tanker Atlantic Asphalt was heading upriver when it slammed into the American Heritage, an American Cruise Lines riverboat that had docked roughly two hours earlier and was preparing to disembark passengers.
- The Rollover: Witnesses watched in shock as the passenger vessel listed sharply before rolling onto its side against the dock within about 15 minutes of the strike, leaving large sections of the boat submerged.
- Rescue in 66-Degree Water: Video from the scene showed passengers in life jackets struggling in the 66-degree river while others clung to the railings of the tilting boat. Rescue boats pulled more than a dozen people directly from the water, while evacuated guests were brought inside the Port of New Orleans Administration Building for triage and medical evaluation.
New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno confirmed that multiple rescues had been made and that search operations remained active.
River Shutdown and Official Response
To keep emergency crews safe and clear the waterway, the U.S. Coast Guard shut down commercial vessel traffic along a three-mile stretch of the Mississippi River between mile markers 93 and 96 — a critical shipping artery connecting inland ports to the Gulf of Mexico.
- State & Federal Briefing: Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry announced he was traveling to New Orleans to coordinate with local law enforcement and emergency officials. A senior White House official also confirmed that President Donald Trump has been briefed on the crash.
- No Confirmed Spill: So far, officials have reported no verified hazardous-material leaks from the tanker, though investigators will closely inspect its cargo holds.
What Happens Next
The U.S. Coast Guard is leading the investigation into how a commercial tanker struck a stationary passenger vessel in broad daylight — examining vessel tracking data, radio communications, river currents, and whether the Atlantic Asphalt suffered a mechanical or steering failure.
For now, the immediate priority remains completing a full headcount of all passengers and crew, treating the injured, and determining how to safely stabilize the partially submerged riverboat.

NEW ORLEANS (AP) — A tanker in New Orleans that apparently lost its steering slammed into a docked river cruise boat with 180 people aboard Friday, the mayor said. All aboard survived after the crash prompted a massive rescue operation for passengers and crew who plunged into the Mississippi River as the ship took on water and began to topple over.
>>> PHOTOS: Rescue crews respond after tanker hits river cruise boat in New Orleans <<<
Video from the scene showed the much larger Atlantic Asphalt tanker hit the cruise boat while it was docked as metal and glass crashed and crunched.
Tugboat operators, nearby workers, police and other rescuers rushed to help.
“We have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi,” New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said at a news conference as rescuers and others cheered.
The mayor said 32 people were taken to the hospital, but none of them had critical injuries.
The American Heritage frequents Pittsburgh, a popular stop on the river boat cruise.
The photo below shows the American Heritage in Pittsburgh on Aug. 22, 2025.
Paddleboat started listing within minutes
The boat started listing within minutes and flipped while emergency workers were still trying to get everyone off the ship.
Dozens of people on board and at least two police officers were dragged from the 66-degree Fahrenheit (19-degree Celsius) river onto nearby ships.
Devon Flanagan was at his job nearby at the Port of New Orleans when workers rushed down the dock. He got out of his truck and saw the American Heritage on its side and passengers in the water.
“It was just chaos,” he said. “You had all types of ships, like other barges and other companies down there trying to help out, which also was a little convoluted because you had people still in the water.”
It appeared the tanker seemed to have “some type of loss of steering,” but the exact cause of the crash was unknown, Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said.
The National Transportation Safety Board planned to investigate the crash, but members were initially unable to make it to New Orleans because all flights nationwide were grounded due to communications problems at regional air traffic control centers.
Cruise line did a roll call to make sure all were accounted for
The people who weren’t injured were brought to a nearby auditorium, and cruise officials did a roll call to make sure everyone was accounted for, Moreno said.
Many people lost their IDs and even car keys in the disaster. Most were from out of town, the mayor said.
“They needed chargers for their phones. Some people didn’t have phones,” Moreno said. “This has now made national news. They need to contact their families to let them know they’re OK. Food, hotel rooms, transportation.”
The cruise ship was built in 2015 and operated by American Cruise Lines. It is five stories and can hold up to 150 passengers.
The American Heritage was finishing an eight-day cruise to several Mississippi River destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi.
The 520-foot-long (160-meter-long) vessel had a final destination in New Orleans, according to MarineTraffic, and was sailing under a flag for the Marshall Islands.
Expert says catastrophic failure of systems on boat
It’s too early to tell what might have caused the crash, but videos indicate some kind of catastrophic system failure on the vessel and “super bad luck” that it struck the boat as passengers were departing, said Martin Davies, a maritime law expert at Tulane University.
The tanker was traveling upriver, going slowly against the current, Davies said.
“For something like this to happen for an upbound ship indicates that something must have gone really badly wrong,” Davies said.
Tankers have local pilots on board for guidance because they know the waters and the ship very well, and the ship had already made the difficult Algiers Point turn on the Mississippi River before it crashed, Davies said.
Tanker owned by subsidiary of Chinese shipbuilder
The tanker is owned by a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation, a sprawling Chinese state-owned conglomerate, according to the website MarineTraffic.
The subsidiary is registered in Liberia and lists no other vessels, but the Chinese company overseeing the asphalt tanker in 2022 accounted for nearly a quarter of the global commercial shipbuilding market, according to a report by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. It was also the largest military shipbuilder in the world at the time.
China State Shipbuilding Corporation didn’t respond to an emailed request for comment on Friday afternoon.
During his first term, President Donald Trump listed the China State Shipbuilding Corporation as one of more than two dozen Chinese-owned companies he accused of exploiting “United States investors to finance the development and modernization” of the Chinese military.
The executive order didn’t freeze all economic transactions for the flagged companies; instead, it placed limits on the types of transactions that these companies could participate in on U.S. soil.

By JACK BROOK, Associated Press
NEW ORLEANS — A tanker in New Orleans that apparently lost its steering slammed into a docked river cruise boat with 180 people aboard Friday, the mayor said. All aboard survived after the crash prompted a massive rescue operation for passengers and crew who plunged into the Mississippi River as the ship took on water and began to topple over.
Video from the scene showed the much larger Atlantic Asphalt tanker hit the cruise boat while it was docked as metal and glass crashed and crunched.
Tugboat operators, nearby workers, police and other rescuers rushed to help.
“We have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi,” New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said at a news conference as rescuers and others cheered.
The mayor said 32 people were taken to the hospital, but none of them had critical injuries.
Paddleboat started listing within minutes
The boat started listing within minutes and flipped while emergency workers were still trying to get everyone off the ship.
Dozens of people on board and at least two police officers were dragged from the 66-degree river onto nearby ships.
Devon Flanagan was at his job nearby at the Port of New Orleans when workers rushed down the dock. He got out of his truck and saw the American Heritage on its side and passengers in the water.
“It was just chaos,” he said. “You had all types of ships, like other barges and other companies down there trying to help out, which also was a little convoluted because you had people still in the water.”
It appeared the tanker seemed to have “some type of loss of steering,” but the exact cause of the crash was unknown, Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said.
The National Transportation Safety Board planned to investigate the crash, but members were initially unable to make it to New Orleans because all flights nationwide were grounded due to communications problems at regional air traffic control centers.
Cruise line did a roll call to make sure all were accounted for
The people who weren’t injured were brought to a nearby auditorium, and cruise officials did a roll call to make sure everyone was accounted for, Moreno said.
Many people lost their IDs and even car keys in the disaster. Most were from out of town, the mayor said.
“They needed chargers for their phones. Some people didn’t have phones,” Moreno said. “This has now made national news. They need to contact their families to let them know they’re OK. Food, hotel rooms, transportation.”
The cruise ship was built in 2015 and operated by American Cruise Lines. It is five stories and can hold up to 150 passengers.
The American Heritage was finishing an eight-day cruise to several Mississippi River destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi.
The 520-foot-long vessel had a final destination in New Orleans, according to MarineTraffic, and was sailing under a flag for the Marshall Islands.
Expert says catastrophic failure of systems on boat
It’s too early to tell what might have caused the crash, but videos indicate some kind of catastrophic system failure on the vessel and “super bad luck” that it struck the boat as passengers were departing, said Martin Davies, a maritime law expert at Tulane University.
The tanker was traveling upriver, going slowly against the current, Davies said.
“For something like this to happen for an upbound ship indicates that something must have gone really badly wrong,” Davies said.
Tankers have local pilots on board for guidance because they know the waters and the ship very well, and the ship had already made the difficult Algiers Point turn on the Mississippi River before it crashed, Davies said.
The tanker is owned by a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation, a sprawling Chinese state-owned conglomerate, according to the website MarineTraffic.
The subsidiary is registered in Liberia and lists no other vessels, but the Chinese company overseeing the asphalt tanker in 2022 accounted for nearly a quarter of the global commercial shipbuilding market, according to a report by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. It was also the largest military shipbuilder in the world at the time.
China State Shipbuilding Corporation didn’t respond to an emailed request for comment on Friday afternoon.
During his first term, President Donald Trump listed the China State Shipbuilding Corporation as one of more than two dozen Chinese-owned companies he accused of exploiting “United States investors to finance the development and modernization” of the Chinese military.
The executive order didn’t freeze all economic transactions for the flagged companies; instead, it placed limits on the types of transactions that these companies could participate in on U.S. soil.
The tanker involved in the crash specializes in carrying large quantities of asphalt and bitumen, a semi-solid substance that is often used for road construction and roofing, according to the live shipping tracker MarineTraffic.
